Tech Report: LATAM Unveils Newly introduced Airbus A321XLR Business Class Suites, Coming March 2027

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft.
  • LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027.
  • The airline intends to use these planes to open up upcoming long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the newly introduced long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

The airline intends to use these planes to open up upcoming long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”.

Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

We can expect LATAM to offer an all-upcoming passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline aims to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:.

Industry observers note that throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV shows. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

It also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

Recent findings suggest that LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

The A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

Recent findings suggest that while American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being remarked, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”.

While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

In early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline plans to use to grow into new markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

According to recent reports, ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is presently offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two fresh wide body business class products over the past several years.

What do you make of LATAM’s new A321XLR business class?

Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card debuted in March 2026.
  • However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee.
  • According to recent reports, this post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card debuted in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

According to recent reports, this post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card.

Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:.

Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:.

With the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited at the moment has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

Admittedly the spending requirement is major (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

According to recent reports, anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

In a recent development, when it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

According to recent reports, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee. Still, that’s a rather steep authorized user fee for a card that doesn’t actually offer many incremental perks. You can add up to 99 employee cards to your account.

Industry observers note that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has no preset spending limit. The idea is that this gives you flexibility in ways that traditional credit cards don’t. The amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history. Rather than having a set limit, you could grow your purchasing power the more you consistently use your card and regularly make payments.

According to recent reports, in fairness, it is also worth mentioning that not having a preset spending limit can also lead to some declines if the amount you can charge decreases, so it’s a little less predictable than a regular credit card. However, I find that more often than not, it works in the favor of cardmembers.

No Preset Spending Limit means your spending limit is flexible. Unlike a traditional card with a set limit, the amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history.

According to recent reports, in terms of its rewards structure, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers 2% cash back on eligible purchases. On top of that, the card offers 5% cash back on flights and prepaid hotels booked through American Express Travel® Online. Just to do some very basic math:.

Industry observers note that all cash back on the card is earned as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases. Unfortunately there are no other redemption options, so you couldn’t directly deposit the cash back into a business checking account, or anything like that.

2% cash back on credit card spending is the “gold standard,” as I see it, so that’s excellent, and what everyone should be aiming for, at a minimum.

In a recent development, meanwhile the 5% cash back on Amex Travel might sound appealing, but there are some catches. If you can route travel spending that way, it’s a good option, but the catch is that you may sometimes find lower rates elsewhere, so there could be an opportunity cost to booking that way.

It has been revealed that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Statement credits will be applied to the monthly bill charged to the card for Amex’s accounts payable solution, One AP, for the following calendar year, and this includes an auto-renewing platform access fee.

American Express One AP® is an accounts payable solution that can help transform the way your business pays suppliers. With One AP, you can streamline your supplier invoice payments on a single platform and pay by virtual card, check, and ACH. Enrollment is required.

Industry observers note that this program charges a $200 monthly fee to pay vendors with non-cards, plus has a fee for checks and ACHs over a certain limit. So the $2,400 annual credit can potentially fully cover your monthly fee. While this is potentially a nice feature, keep in mind that many platforms already offer this as a built in feature at no extra cost, so it’s not really that special.

Sources indicate that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers the Pay Over Time feature, whereby cardmembers can carry a balance with interest on eligible charges, up to the Pay Over Time limit. The way this works, eligible charges will automatically be added to a Pay Over Time balance, up to the Pay Over Time limit.

You can choose to pay for these charges over time with interest, or you can pay your full balance each month, whichever is best for your business. You must pay in full any charge or a portion of a charge that is not added to a Pay Over Time balance.

Personally, I recommend paying the balance in full each billing cycle if possible, to avoid interest charges, especially given how high they can be. However, I think it’s worth clarifying that the Pay Over Time option is possible, given that this isn’t a traditional credit card.

It’s also worth emphasizing the difference between the Pay Over Time and the Pay In Full Limit. The latter could be an amount that has to be paid in full, and there’s no option to pay that over time with interest charges.

According to recent reports, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card earns 2% cash back, and I consider that to be the minimum “gold standard” of credit card rewards. So the card’s rewards structure is perfectly fine. The 5% cash back on travel is also pretty limiting, given that you have to book through Amex.

Sources indicate that I think the issue is the steep annual fee, given that there are also much more affordable (and even no annual fee) cards with that kind of a rewards structure. In fairness, Amex doesn’t have another business card earning unlimited 2% cash back. It’s just not a latest concept more broadly, and there are lots of competing cards that I’d consider to be superior.

Sources indicate that so who should consider the card? As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is targeted at a specific demographic. This card could make sense for the following types of customers:.

I do truly think this is a niche product. But the idea is that if you’re a small business owner charging hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars on credit cards per year, that annual fee won’t make much of a difference.

Still, I’d like to compare this to some other popular products, as I think there are other cards that may be a better fit for some other people.

Perhaps the best direct comparison to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1% cash back thereafter).

The upside here is obvious, as you’re earning 2% cash back with no fee. The downside is that the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

For a small business mostly spending money domestically, the Amex Blue Business Cash is a great alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash.

Recent findings suggest that another potential alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1x points thereafter).

In a recent development, if you’re good at redeeming points, that’s a pretty incredible return, since based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, for a return of up to 3.4%. The downsides to the Amex Blue Business Plus are otherwise identical to those on the Amex Blue Business Cash — the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2x points on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

So the card is either useful if $50,000 covers your annual business spending, or you’re willing to use another card after you hit that initial $50,000 spending cap.

Speaking of premium Amex business cards, it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the American Express® Business Gold Card (learn more). The Amex Business Gold has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers an incredible rewards structure (with up to 4x Membership Rewards points in select categories), plus statement credits that can greatly help offset the annual fee.

As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is the better option if you value cash back and a straightforward rewards structure, while the Amex Business Gold is the better option if you can take advantage of the bonus categories, and are willing to put in the effort to maximize points.

While the above comparisons are all to Amex cards, I think it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Capital One Spark Cash Plus (learn more), as it’s perhaps the most direct competitor.

In a recent development, the card has a massive welcome offer of $2,000 cash back after spending $30,000 within the first three months (plus an additional $2,000 cash back bonus for every $500,000 spent during the first year), offers 5% cash back on select Capital One Business Travel purchases and 2% cash back with no caps and no foreign transaction fees on other purchases, and it has a $150 annual fee. Furthermore, the card offers an annual bonus of $150 if you spend at least $150,000 on the card in a calendar year, essentially rebating the annual fee.

I do think the Capital One Spark Cash Plus is more compelling than the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card on balance, unless you specifically have a reason you’d like an Amex, or value the statement credits tied to spending $250,000 per year.

I’d also like to compare the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (learn more), as it’s another potentially lucrative cash back card.

In addition to a massive welcome offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 within the first three months, the card offers 5% cash back on Chase Travel purchases, 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more, and 2% cash back on all other purchases, with no foreign transaction fees, and it has a $195 annual fee. So if you have a business that frequently makes large purchases, the Chase Ink Business Premier could be a great alternative.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card has a $295 annual fee, and offers unlimited 2% cash back, with no preset spending limit, plus a large welcome offer. The card also offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year.

Ultimately I’d consider this to be a niche card. The card could be worth getting for the excellent welcome offer, and it could be worth it if you have a business that spends a huge amount, and values the lack of a preset spending limit, the card’s Amex branding, and/or the statement credits.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, though, I tend to think there are better options. If you’re not a huge spender, the Amex Blue Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Plus are excellent options. If you’re willing to maximize points and bonus categories, consider the Amex Business Gold. And if you’re looking for the best direct alternative that’s arguably more lucrative, consider the Capital One Spark Cash Plus.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of concerns even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, mentioned Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    It has been revealed that still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin?     💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Trump has revived a claim that his private pilot previously relied on another country's air traffic control (ATC) system while flying in the US, prompting a public rebuttal from a private pilot.
    • In a recent development, the comments came one week after a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted thousands of flights and just days after the administration requested another $50.1 billion for aviation modernization.
    • According to the Daily Beast, Trump made the remarks during a "bonkers appearance" at a White House press conference addressing recent disruptions involving aviation, banking and communications networks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Trump has revived a claim that his private pilot previously relied on another country's air traffic control (ATC) system while flying in the US, prompting a public rebuttal from a private pilot. Speaking during a White House press conference on Friday, Trump criticized America's aviation infrastructure while discussing recent disruptions affecting the country's airspace, according to National Public Radio (NPR).

    In a recent development, the comments came one week after a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted thousands of flights and just days after the administration requested another $50.1 billion for aviation modernization. However, Trump's account of using foreign controllers has raised questions about whether he meant air traffic control or the navigation technology installed aboard his aircraft.

    According to the Daily Beast, Trump made the remarks during a "bonkers appearance" at a White House press conference addressing recent disruptions involving aviation, banking and communications networks. Asked about the incidents, the president maintained that they were unrelated, before discussing his personal experiences with private aviation.

    Trump described US ATC infrastructure as "ancient", and said that his pilot had used foreign air traffic control before he entered office.

    “It's ancient! In fact, you know, before I was here, I had a plane. I had a very nice life. And my pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country. This was years ago, before I was in office. I don't want to say the country, but he found one country better than ours.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the assertion prompted a response from journalist Brian Karem, who identified himself as a private pilot. In a post on X, Karem disputed the suggestion that pilots operating in US airspace could bypass domestic controllers by seeking assistance from another country. His objection centered on the distinction between the authorities controlling airspace and the equipment pilots use to navigate.

    Recent findings suggest that "You cannot call up ATC in Europe and say, 'Hey give me a hand. I'm flying over US airspace.'".

    It has been revealed that trump's remarks were not entirely new. During the National Prayer Breakfast in February last year, he similarly claimed to use equipment or services from another country when landing his private aircraft in New York, according to Anadolu Ajansı. The comments attracted scrutiny from aviation experts at the time, Forbes reported.

    President Trump likely confused air traffic control systems with onboard navigation technology, according to Forbes. Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox explained that pilots operating under ATC supervision must comply with the applicable rules of that country, regardless of their navigation equipment's country of origin.

    Air traffic control and aircraft navigation perform very different functions. Controllers matter clearances, instructions and traffic information, while onboard navigation systems help pilots determine their position and follow flight plans. An aircraft operating under instrument flight rules in controlled US airspace cannot simply select a foreign ATC provider. The differences are summarized below:.

    Provides clearances, traffic separation and instructions.

    Provides satellite-based positioning and navigation.

    Calculates and manages the aircraft's flight path.

    Inertial reference system (IRS).

    Tracks aircraft position and movement using onboard sensors.

    Provide route, waypoint and procedure information.

    Provide navigation, communication or flight management capabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that A plausible explanation is that Trump's aircraft used internationally manufactured avionics, navigation databases, or satellite-based positioning technology. As the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Aeronautical Information Manual explains, these technologies provide navigation guidance but do not replace ATC services. Without confirmation from Trump's former pilots, the precise technology he was describing remains unknown.

    According to recent reports, the dispute comes amid growing pressure to modernize the FAA's aging infrastructure. On November 13, a telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop lasting nearly five hours. According to the FAA's subsequent investigation, excessive network traffic destabilized legacy equipment, affecting communications and radar feeds at 17 of the country's 22 enroute control centers. Approximately 12,500 flights were canceled that day, and hundreds more over the days that followed.

    On November 17, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and Budget Director Russell Vought formally requested $50.1 billion from Congress. The proposal follows $12.5 billion approved in July 2025 and would finance technology upgrades, replacement facilities, and airport infrastructure. The administration's request is broken down as follows:.

    ATC technology and digital modernization.

    Airport infrastructure improvements.

    Five consolidated enroute control centers.

    Construction and upgrades of up to 140 ATC towers.

    In a recent development, the FAA aims to complete the first phase of its Brand New Air Traffic Control System by December 2028. However, in September, the Government Accountability Office warned that incomplete cost estimates and scheduling would undermine progress. Although the need for modernization is well documented, it does not establish that foreign controllers previously managed Trump's flights within US airspace. The president's renewed remarks therefore leave the original technical question unresolved.

    • However, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced?
    • Airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.

    However, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced? Well, or perhaps more accurately, they are enforced, but using very dishonest math. The backstory of this is interesting.

    Airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal. An airport is like a shopping mall with a very captive audience, and as you’d expect, rent for businesses in airports is absolutely through the roof, as a result of that.

    According to recent reports, but in order to balance things out and prevent retailers from exploiting consumers, over 80% of airports in the United States specifically stipulate the maximum prices that airports can charge consumers. These terms are typically baked into the contracts that airport retailers sign, and failure to adhere to the rules can lead to consequences, at least in theory.

    The airports with pricing caps for airport businesses generally fall into one of two categories:.

    If there are supposed to be rules in place capping airport pricing, then why is this such a widespread glitch? More Perfect Union recently published a great video investigating this issue, and it’s a fascinating watch. First they actually analyze airport pricing, and then they confront airport authorities about the lack of enforcement.

    Here’s what’s interesting — airport retailers do have to submit comparisons for benchmark pricing, to prove that they’re not violating rules and exploiting customers. The matter is what kind of businesses are considered comparable for the purposes of “street pricing.”.

    For example, 9NEWS recently investigated this at Denver Airport, finding that a basic Starbucks coffee cost $4.55 in the airport, compared to $2.95 outside the airport (a 54% markup), and a bag of cashews cost $9.99 in the airport, compared to $4.74 outside the airport (a 110% markup).

    The airport’s VP of Concessions agreed to sit down with the reporter to discuss this, and she said the results of his investigation were great news — she suggested that 93% of the prices were compliant, and said “that’s pretty darn good.” How could that be, given the high markups compared to nearby businesses?

    The glitch boils down to how much latitude businesses have to submit pricing comparisons:.

    What’s wild is how the airport official responds to Starbucks just having consistent pricing, and violating the rules:.

    Sources indicate that VP of Concessions: “What I get from that is, they’re looking for consistency, across the board, across the nation, across the world.”Reporter: “I can’t help but think that travelers may be looking for consistency, but if they see a cheaper cup of coffee, they’ll probably be okay with it.”VP of Concessions: “I don’t know the answer to that. This is how we take care of our passengers, by ensuring that they are paying fair and transparent pricing, while supporting our business partners.”.

    Back to the original story, the More Perfect Union reporter confronted the Port Authority of Newly introduced York and New Jersey about pricing like $6.89 for one liter of Smart Water, compared to closer to $3.50 at nearby bodegas.

    The response was that “comparing a Hudson to a bodega isn’t appropriate,” because “Hudson is a specialty market.” The approved price comparison was reportedly based on the price of water at Tablet Works, a “wellness & concierge pharmacy” in a high-end mall.

    The other thing to keep in mind is that a large percentage of airport retailers and restaurants are run by the same few companies, like HMSHost, which is a subsidiary of Avolta. So clearly they have a centralized approach to submitting pricing comparisons, and know exactly what they’re doing. Interestingly, the few independent businesses in some airports were found to have the most honest pricing.

    So to sum it up, the system is designed to be rigged. Airport authorities can technically pretend they’re looking out for consumers by setting a cap. Retailers can submit pricing comparisons to the highest prices they can find anywhere. Then airport authorities verify those prices to pretend they’re doing their jobs.

    Airports are obviously complicit in all of this. They make money by charging sky high rent, and the reason they can do that is because retailers can charge hugely inflated prices. The more profits retailers make, the more airports can charge in rent. And they know that no consumer is going to avoid an airport because of high concession costs.

    Around 80% of airports in the United States cap the prices that retailers can charge, so in most cases, you’re not supposed to be paying more than 15% above “street pricing.” The glitch is the liberties that businesses can take with what constitutes “street pricing.”.

    The price of the bottle of water or smoothie you’re buying isn’t compared to what you’d pay at a nearby gas station and smoothie shop, but instead, is being compared to what you’d pay at Erewhon. Talk about a very broken system, with no incentives for any party to actually be honest….

    What do you make of this airport pricing situation?

    #19600. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, noted they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    Industry observers note that “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    It has been revealed that thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz remarked. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they remarked.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer noted they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about aims for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter mentioned.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    It has been revealed that “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related concerns,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján stated, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    Sources indicate that “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that problem,” Moran noted.

    Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    #19599. Tech Report: Why The Flying Wing Never Became A Commercial Airliner

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1502 w)

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Why The Flying Wing Never Became A Commercial Airliner

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, jack Northrop envisioned a sleek, tailless future when he sent the YB-49 aloft on October 21, 1947, stretching a 172-foot (52.4 meters) wing across the desert sky without a conventional fuselage or vertical stabilizer.
    • Despite the allure of an all-wing silhouette, commercial aviation stuck with cylindrical fuselages and tailed configurations that offered predictable handling, straightforward cabin pressurization, and familiar airport compatibility.
    • In a recent development, converted from two piston-engined YB-35 airframes, the YB-49 stretched to a 172-foot (52.4-meter) wingspan and measured 53 feet, 1 inch (16.2 meters) in length, trading propeller drives for eight Allison J35 turbojets buried inside the wing, according to The Little Aviation Museum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, jack Northrop envisioned a sleek, tailless future when he sent the YB-49 aloft on October 21, 1947, stretching a 172-foot (52.4 meters) wing across the desert sky without a conventional fuselage or vertical stabilizer. Promising lower drag and greater efficiency than traditional layouts, the experimental jet bomber nevertheless battled stability challenges before the second prototype crashed on June 5, 1948, killing all five crew members aboard and leading to the program winding down between 1949 and 1950.

    Despite the allure of an all-wing silhouette, commercial aviation stuck with cylindrical fuselages and tailed configurations that offered predictable handling, straightforward cabin pressurization, and familiar airport compatibility. Now that digital flight controls and blended-wing concepts are bringing tailless aerodynamics back into the spotlight, what technical, operational, and commercial hurdles still stand between a flying wing concept and a viable passenger airliner?

    In a recent development, converted from two piston-engined YB-35 airframes, the YB-49 stretched to a 172-foot (52.4-meter) wingspan and measured 53 feet, 1 inch (16.2 meters) in length, trading propeller drives for eight Allison J35 turbojets buried inside the wing, according to The Little Aviation Museum. Removing a conventional fuselage and tail assembly allowed almost the entire planform to contribute to lift with reduced parasite drag, helping the prototype reach roughly 493 mph (793 km/h). At the same time, early turbojet fuel burn and internal volume tradeoffs tempered its range and payload flexibility relative to piston-powered designs.

    Flying without a tall vertical tail meant the YB-49 had less natural stability in yaw and had delicate pitch and roll-yaw coupling, including dutch roll, during turbulent air, maneuvers, and simulated bombing runs. As noted by MiGFlug, four small vertical fins were fitted to aid directional damping, though in the late 1940s crews relied on mechanical linkages and human coordination rather than high-speed digital flight control computers to manage continuous stability corrections.

    After its maiden flight on October 21, 1947, the program flew only two converted airframes before the second prototype crashed on June 5, 1948, claiming the lives of all five crew members on board. Production orders were canceled in 1949 as Air Force leadership shifted toward competing bomber programs, and formal flight testing concluded in March 1950 before the surviving airframes were scrapped.

    For an aerodynamically unstable tailless wing to become a dependable aircraft and actually work, it requires replacing purely mechanical linkages with high-speed digital fly-by-wire flight-control computers. Motion sensors can continuously measure aircraft attitude and rate changes, feeding real-time data to flight computers that command rapid, micro-adjusted deflections across trailing-edge control surfaces. That closed-loop automation damps pitch, yaw, and dutch roll oscillations far faster and more consistently than manual pilot inputs alone could achieve in earlier eras.

    Sources indicate that digital flight control design made the Northrop B-2 Spirit possible by allowing a pure flying wing to achieve low-observable radar signatures without needing a conventional vertical tail. Instead of using a large fin that would compromise stealth, the B-2 uses computer-coordinated elevons and split drag rudders to generate controlled yawing moments and maintain crisp handling across varying weights and flight regimes. Computing redundancy and sensor voting became foundational to keeping a naturally neutral or unstable wing profile predictable from takeoff through landing.

    Decades later, the Northrop B-21 Raider extends that digital control lineage into a modern low-observable bomber program built on newer avionics and computing architectures. The B-2 and B-21 demonstrate that computerized flight controls conquered the core stability and control challenges of tailless military aircraft, but solving stability in a combat airframe did not automatically translate into an airline cabin, and how to make it a reality.

    The pure flying wing has not necessarily been revived, but JetZero is advancing the Z4 as a blended wing body (BWB) concept designed to carry roughly 230 to 250 passengers by smoothly merging a wide, lifting center body into outer wings. The program has gained traction through a $235 million US Air Force award supporting full-scale demonstrator development alongside plans to establish manufacturing operations in North Carolina. With a full-scale demonstrator targeted to fly in late 2027, the roadmap aims for commercial entry into service in the early 2030s if technical and regulatory hurdles are cleared on schedule.

    Commercial interest in the Z4 is very real, and carriers such as Japan Airlines and United Airlines have made agreements to support the development of the aircraft. For airlines evaluating next-generation single-aisle and midsize replacements, a BWB promises lower drag and reduced fuel burn per seat compared with conventional tube-and-wing layouts. Making those conditional fleet commitments become firm deliveries, however, depends on proving that the airframe can meet strict safety, manufacturing, and operational standards at scale.

    Recent findings suggest that propulsion integration sits near the center of that verification effort, including a November 2026 report from Leeham News noting that the FAA is funding a study into top-mounted engine airflow for JetZero's design. Placing engines above the aft airframe can help shield noise, but maintaining clean airflow and stable engine operation across flight conditions remains a critical engineering focus ahead of commercial certification.

    According to recent reports, A cylindrical tube naturally resists internal cabin pressure by distributing hoop stress evenly around a circular cross-section, whereas a wide, flattened wing-body hull faces far higher bending and pressure-loading demands. A non-cylindrical cabin shell tends to bow outward when pressurized at cruise altitude, so to compensate, designers need to add structural reinforcement, internal bulkheads, or load-bearing frames that add mass and complexity.

    In a recent development, emergency evacuation rules further add to cabin design complexity, particularly the regulatory requirement to evacuate a full aircraft within 90 seconds using half of the available exits, covered in Simple Flying analysis. Unlike a narrow single- or twin-aisle tube where passengers move linearly toward well-marked doors, a wide blended-wing cabin needs carefully engineered pathways, clear signage, and balanced exit placement, so travelers seated deep inside the layout can reach exits without bottlenecks. Cabin tiering across premium and economy zones also needs to align with aisle geometry and exit capacity rather than treating interior floor space as an open hall.

    Industry observers note that on the ground, widebody wingspans around 213 feet (65 meters) must fit within existing terminal gate envelopes, taxiway clearances, and apron stand markings without forcing costly airport rebuilds. Even when a wide airframe clears wingspan limits at a standard widebody gate, its broader center section and altered fuselage contour can complicate jetbridge docking reach, de-icing access, and ground support vehicle positioning. Smooth ramp operations really depend on proving that turnaround tasks load and unload cleanly alongside conventional airliners.

    In a recent development, within a wide, open cabin, the sensory rhythm of a flight changes compared with walking down a narrow, low-ceilinged aisle. Designers can shape the atmosphere through layered ambient lighting, tactile fabrics, and warmer material palettes that soften the industrial feel of long-haul travel and create distinct zones for rest, work, or socializing. When the interior feels less like a corridor and more like a curated living space, passenger stress often eases.

    Sightlines and motion perception play a major role in whether that spaciousness feels inviting or disorienting. Travelers seated further outboard from the centerline can notice more pronounced vertical movement when the aircraft banks or hits chop, making smooth cabin damping and calm visual anchors especially valuable. At the same time, passengers placed in central rows away from outer walls miss natural views of the horizon, requiring thoughtful lighting cues or digital view panels to keep the cabin feeling open and grounded.

    For airlines, an unconventional cabin layout offers a rare canvas for brand differentiation in a crowded market. Carriers can build an identity around quiet acoustics, signature color schemes, and tailored service rituals that signal innovation without feeling gimmicky. If passengers connect emotionally with the warmth and poise of the space, the cabin itself becomes part of the airline's promise, not something that needs to be explained to customers.

    Pure flying wings remained absent from passenger service because winning aerodynamic efficiency on paper is only half the battle when weighed against structural pressure loads, emergency evacuation rules, airport compatibility, and airline economics. Digital flight controls solved the stability hurdles that haunted the YB-49 and paved the way for stealth bombers, but turning a wide, wing-shaped cabin into a profitable, certified airliner is no easy task.

    Any manufacturer brave enough to try and make something like this has to solve practical constraints that circular fuselages and conventional tails handle with far less friction. Whether a blended wing body can actually fill that divide comes down to proving real-world reliability, passenger acceptance, and unit economics without turning every airport gate or cabin layout into a costly exception.

    The next major checkpoints arrive with full-scale demonstrator flight testing targeted for late 2027 and potential commercial entry into service in the early 2030s. If JetZero or other ventures like Nautilus can validate aerodynamic performance, propulsion integration, and regulatory certification along that timeline, blended-wing designs could finally move from aviation curiosity to active airline fleets.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

    While I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

    In a recent development, well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has unveiled plans to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a new global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

    According to recent reports, as is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:.

    In a recent development, emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

    Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:.

    “Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This latest First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”.

    In a recent development, we’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary upcoming first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

    Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:.

    According to recent reports, featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

    When it comes to the temporary fresh first class lounge, here are the details:.

    As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉.

    According to recent reports, but when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

    Two things stand out to me here:.

    Emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s new lounge aesthetic.

    We’ve just seen the opening of a newly introduced temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

    In a recent development, the new design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We swiftly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

    The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.

    So, what’s actually going on here? A latest report sheds some more light on this….

    CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

    In a recent development, according to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

    That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications issues across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

    FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”.

    Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

    It has been revealed that this type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”.

    With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

    Industry observers note that while the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

    A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”.

    That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

    It has been revealed that while the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door.     The good news is that there’s a huge incentive to apply for the card, given the massive limited-time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card is undergoing some major updates. This includes a higher annual fee, latest rewards structure, and new set of perks. However, these changes only apply to new card members, as existing card members will keep the old benefits (and fee).

    In a recent development, let me emphasize that the card has a huge limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. So that’s a major incentive to apply for the card, if you’re eligible. I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so to me, that’s worth $1,350.

    With that out of the way, let’s go over the details….

    Sources indicate that the Atmos Rewards Business Card now has a flat $195 annual fee, which covers the primary card member and any employee cards. Previously, the card had an annual fee of $70 per company, plus $25 per employee, so the minimum annual fee you’d pay would be $95.

    It goes without saying that this change represents a significant increase in the annual fee, unless you had more than four employee credit cards on your account.

    Industry observers note that the Atmos Rewards Business Card also has a new rewards structure. The card now offers:.

    In a recent development, what has changed here is the fresh 10x points for booking through Atmos for Business (great for those who can use it), as well as a full overhaul of the 2x points categories. Previously the card offered 2x points on eligible gas, EV charging stations, shipping, and local transit purchases (including rideshare), while now it just offers 2x points on dining. As before, the card offers one status point for every $3 spent, with no cap.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card is picking up quite a few upcoming benefits that it didn’t previously offer:.

    The refreshed card also keeps a first checked bag free and preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights for the card member and up to six guests on the same reservation when the trip is paid with the card, a 20% rebate on eligible inflight purchases, a 10% rewards bonus for cardholders with an eligible Bank of America small business account, and no foreign transaction fees.

    Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the new 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

    As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a new Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

    Applications submitted before November 18 will continue under the prior card offering. What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

    As of now, it sounds like there are no intends to transition people to the upcoming system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

    Industry observers note that the Atmos Rewards Business Card changes are a mixed bag. First, I want to once again emphasize that since existing card members aren’t impacted by these changes, I don’t think there should be too much frustration here.

    In the past, the Atmos Rewards Business Card basically felt like the business version of the $95 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more), while now the card feels more like a hybrid between that and the $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), in terms of both cost and benefits.

    So I don’t have a terribly strong take here, other than wishing that spending on the card were a bit more lucrative, and more competitive with what’s offered by the Atmos Rewards Summit Card. The Summit Card will continue to be my go-to card for Atmos Rewards.

    • Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Industry observers note that saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen.
    • Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Industry observers note that saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders noted Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care initiative if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

    Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

    Industry observers note that sanders mentioned Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

    According to recent reports, his version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

    The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

    “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders remarked, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

    According to recent reports, sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

    According to recent reports, while who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders remarked he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

    Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

    Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    According to recent reports, in addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

    To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

    Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., stated last week that he intends to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

    Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee problems, he looks forward to finding common ground.
