    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Among all the gruesome details of allegations both old and fresh of rape and sexual abuse, there’s one four-word phrase in the new congressional report on Jeffrey Epstein that claims a lot about why Donald Trump seems especially unhinged these days: “No statute of limitations.” Led by Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee released their findings on the president’s long and close relationship with the deceased sex offender. The report, citing testimony from 11 women, “indicates that Trump abused, assaulted, and even raped numerous women alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.”.

    The media response to the allegations was muted, despite compelling latest evidence about the extent of Epstein’s sex trafficking ring, suggesting more powerful men were involved than have faced legal repercussions. Perhaps the report was overshadowed by the midterm elections. Or maybe there’s a sense this is “old news” and won’t move the needle. But if Raskin has his way, we’ll all look back to this release as the opening chapter in a season of accountability not just for Trump, but also for various administration figures and MAGA cronies who have enjoyed the legal shield of a Republican congressional majority.

    Democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, they’ll have access to a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players.

    Sources indicate that democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, Raskin and investigators will have a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players who have been taking full advantage of the atmosphere of corruption the president has created. The Epstein report is likely just the beginning. As the Washington Post noted on Monday, Democrats “are laying the groundwork for an array of inquiries into President Donald Trump, his family and his administration.” Various business and political leaders are meeting with their lawyers, worried about what Democrats could uncover with this newly introduced power.

    “I haven’t seen this much investigative activity in anticipation of a change in control of a house of Congress ever,” Michael Bopp, who runs a congressional investigations division for the law firm Gibson Dunn, told the Post.

    There are plenty of signs that it’s dawning on people around Trump that he will be out of office in two short years and that, as the latest Epstein report indicates, the statute of limitations has not run out on many possible crimes committed under the White House’s protection. A recent Zeteo profile of Stephen Miller revealed that the White House deputy chief of staff is worried about going to prison if a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028. Congressional Democrats keep talking about impeaching Pete Hegseth, and the defense secretary is clearly anxious, reportedly making calls and begging Sen. Marsha Blackburn to appoint him to her Senate seat if, as expected, she wins the Tennessee governor’s race this week. Having a Senate seat would not only prevent impeachment; it could make prosecuting him for alleged war crimes much harder as well.

    In October Elissa Slotkin of Michigan set off a massive panic on the right when she suggested that there should be a focus on “signature cases” against “people who enabled” Trump. The Michigan senator wanted a “deterrence message” for anyone considering working for Trump, letting them know that committing crimes or otherwise assisting in illegal or corrupt activity might result in “a ton of problems” for them that aren’t worth the risk of legal liability. Fox News and other outlets tried to spin this as Slotkin threatening the mass arrest of young staffers, but the hysteria belies their real worry: Democrats might be able to compile enough evidence that prison is a real threat for many of the people working for Trump.

    In a recent development, slotkin’s remarks clearly rattled the White House. Since then, Trump has repeatedly put out word that his underlings should not have to worry about obeying the law because mass pardons are on their way. A few days after Slotkin’s warning, sources inside the White House told the Washington Sun that administration lawyers are looking at “blanket pardons for all employees involved in particular policy areas, such as deportations, war or trade.”.

    Industry observers note that still, the White House is facing serious staffing problems. A September report from the Partnership for Public Service found that people Trump hires rapidly leave. Not only have there been a record number of resignations, nearly half of the quitters worked less than a year for Trump.

    Recent findings suggest that on Monday, Trump himself also told the New York Post that widespread pardons are on the table, not just for his staff, but for allies like Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Musk has good reason to be worried. His brief tenure running DOGE has raised a whole host of questions about what laws were broken by him or by staff carrying out his orders. He’s also under suspicion of messing with Ukraine’s Starlink access, crippling its defenses against the invading Russian military. This may explain why Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars — more than any single donor in history — trying to tilt the elections in the GOP’s favor.

    According to recent reports, trump and his family members should also be sweating. Trump has often interpreted the Supreme Court’s grant of presidential immunity as all-encompassing, but as Raskin told the New Yorker, he doesn’t see it that way at all. He outlined how the president has made billions in office, roughly $1 million a hour, and that there’s a great deal to learn about where that money is coming from. The Supreme Court’s decision technically only covers crimes committed during the commission of official presidential duties. By definition, Trump’s external money-making enterprises aren’t that. His children are deeply involved in the family business as well. And as the Epstein report made sure to note, some of the crimes Trump and his associates have been accused of committing with his old friend Epstein carry no statute of limitations.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    It’s tempting to wave all this off as inconsequential, because Trump and his cronies were able to escape severe ramifications the last time around. But to dismiss this talk would be a mistake, in no small part because Democrats need their feet held to the fire. The corruption this time around is far worse than it was in Trump’s first term, more flagrant as the air of lawlessness led to a level of carelessness that creates more prosecutable evidence. The next Democrat in office may not be like Joe Biden, who shied away from aggressive prosecution of Trump and his allies. Some of the politicians whose names are being bandied around — like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia — have been highly focused weeding out MAGA corruption.

    Sources indicate that then there’s the matter of political will. Before now, it was hard to drum up sufficient political support for accountability because voters simply didn’t care enough about corruption. But as the New York Times reported last week, the issue is a rising source concern for voters. Democrats, for one thing, are doing a better job of linking Trump’s self-dealing to the economic problems of ordinary people. For another, the Epstein scandal has broken into national consciousness, and even Republicans are struggling to sufficiently explain why Trump, despite signing a bill to release all Justice Department files related to the case, is refusing to do so.

    With these winds at their back, Democrats have a much better chance of being able to conduct thorough investigations — and pursue criminal consequences for those found to have broken the law.

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    Industry observers note that “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews mentioned, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” mentioned Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    Industry observers note that “I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Recent findings suggest that peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    According to recent reports, A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” remarked California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he aims to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    Sources indicate that they’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” remarked Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    Sources indicate that RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun released his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but mentioned last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    Industry observers note that newly introduced leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    According to recent reports, remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, revealed a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    According to recent reports, the  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who notes she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the Latest York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    Industry observers note that after Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    Industry observers note that west Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Recent findings suggest that machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly mentioned he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    President Donald Trump fumed at Fox News on Election Day, accusing the conservative network of turning against him, giving Democrats too much airtime and driving away its own viewers.

    It has been revealed that “FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me.”.

    ﻿.

    Trump insisted his own popularity remained strong, claiming his numbers were “better than they have ever been” and citing a CNN poll that he said showed overwhelming Republican support for him.

    The president also accused Fox News of deliberately undermining him through its polling.

    “The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask,” Trump wrote. “Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLS***!'”.

    Industry observers note that his grievances extended beyond the network’s programming. Trump questioned why Fox Corp. was financially supporting Democratic politicians and organizations, naming House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Reps. Jamie Raskin, Ted Lieu and Pete Aguilar, along with several Democratic campaign committees. He did not provide figures to substantiate his allegations.

    Trump also singled out Jessica Tarlov, the Democratic strategist and co-host of Fox News’ “The Five,” with a personal insult while watching the network’s election coverage, a complaint he brought up in previous posts.

    “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me,” Trump wrote, adding that he would change channels until she was off the air.

    Fox News has experienced a ratings decline, although Trump’s explanation for the drop is unsubstantiated. Nielsen data demonstrated the network’s total-day audience fell 27% in October compared with the previous year, according to TheWrap. Fox nevertheless remained the most-watched cable news network.

    Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch attributed the decline to viewer fatigue during an earnings call Monday.

    Trump, however, insisted the network’s coverage of him was responsible.

    In a recent development, “They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!” he wrote. “This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”.

    • Burnham, who entered the world 121 years ago Sunday and left it nearly 40 years ago, very much remains part of the Great Conversation.
    • Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S.

    The British first edition of The Managerial Revolution that I picked up in a Charing Cross Road shop a quarter century ago tells us much about the work itself. I’ve read it four times, conscripted it as an airplane companion, and brought it to the beach. Yet its binding remains strong, its cover quite flexible, and its pages yellowing but intact. We no longer much refer to let alone read such 1941 bestsellers as Clifton Fadiman’s Reading I’ve Liked or Margaret Leech’s Reveille in Washington. But James Burnham, much like my strong and solid copy of his most famous book, endures.

    Burnham, who entered the world 121 years ago Sunday and left it nearly 40 years ago, very much remains part of the Great Conversation. The Managerial Revolution, anticipating as it did the ascension of technocrats, specialists, and the bureaucratic elite as a sort of ruling class, surely helped in that regard. Burnham remains read, despite no Burnhamite clique in academia or organized faction among movement conservatives dedicated to advancing his ideas. Kirkians, Straussians, and Randians exist. Why no James Burnham Preservation Society with an accompanying secret handshake?

    Sources indicate that daniel J. Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S. Meyer, is an American Spectator senior editor, visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution, and YouTuber @RightWingWilderness.

    On “The Complex Reputation of James Burnham”.

    The contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

    The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

    Recent findings suggest that georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

    On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

    Industry observers note that bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., stated earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

    Industry observers note that when former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack remarked that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack mentioned in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he mentioned at Thursday’s meeting.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

    This marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

    The big blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

    A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a upcoming record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

    Although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

    Industry observers note that although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the signs were there from the outset. About 30 minutes after the polls in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District closed at 6 p.m., the first numbers from rural counties began trickling in. It was no surprise that they favored Republican Ralph Alvarado over Democrat Zach Dembo. The district was reliably Democratic until 2012, when Andy Barr, a Republican who is now running to replace Mitch McConnell in the Senate, eked out a win. Since then, the GOP has gerrymandered the district to all but ensure it stayed in the fold.

    The real story, though, could be found in the margins. Alvarado was underperforming Barr’s 2024 results by around 20 percentage points — a staggering drop, indicating that a significant number of Republicans had either stayed home or decided to take a chance on Dembo. Off the Democratic map for the last 14 years, by 9:15 p.m., when it was reported that Alvarado had conceded, the district had become a microcosm of what was unfolding nationwide.

    The blue landslide, long predicted by pundits but mentioned with fingers crossed by Democrats, was becoming an avalanche.

    Industry observers note that further south in Georgia, an earlier-than-expected call for Jon Ossoff buoyed Democratic hopes, followed by a pickup in the North Carolina Senate race, which saw Gov. Roy Cooper projected to defeat former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley. Democrats even put up a fight in ruby-red Florida’s statewide races, with David Jolly, the nominee for governor, and Angie Nixon, the democratic socialist Senate candidate, running ahead of their opponents until the conservative Panhandle’s votes were counted.

    Industry observers note that then came South Carolina, where Darline Graham, who was foisted upon the state’s Republican Party by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, after his death, went down to an historic defeat. The Palmetto State hasn’t seen a Democrat elected to the Senate since 1998.

    Recent findings suggest that amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, routed her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy after he released a widely condemned ad that weaponized a horrific part of her childhood. In Texas, James Talarico is projected for a stunning win over scandal-plagued Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion.

    Other elections around the country — Senate races in Michigan, Kansas and Iowa; pivotal House contests and gubernatorial races — appear to be trending for Democrats.

    For a decade, the party has wondered when, or if, a reckoning would arrive for Trump and MAGA. That moment has arrived.

    Again and again, Republicans have followed the president over the cliff, no more so than during the past 22 months. In 2024, Trump expanded on the coalition that had carried him to success in 2016 by making inroads with Black men, Latinos and young voters. It was a success that, at least in part, led Republicans to launch a national gerrymandering scheme largely thwarted by Democrats, as well as an unfavorable economic climate of the president’s own making.

    It has been revealed that but Trump also made the grievous error of attacking the very communities that helped return him to the White House. The combination of his assaults on voting rights and Black history, as well as the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, ensured that Black voters turned out overwhelmingly for Democrats. After more than a year of ICE raids, mass deportations and threats against naturalized citizens, Latinos have swung to the Democrats en masse, playing a decisive role in Talarico’s win. Trump’s attacks on civil rights, immigrants’ rights and the social safety net have cut across demographic groups, and have had a strong negative impact on young voters. Drunk on his own power, the president has spent the better part of two years splintering his own coalition — and giving Democrats an opening they were happy to exploit.

    The monumental defeat suffered by Republicans offers a sobering lesson for Democrats — to not forget what brought them to this night of victory.

    Sources indicate that the message voters are sending is loud and clear: They want fighters, leaders who are willing to throw out conventional wisdom and do battle for working-class interests. That’s what Ossoff sensed last fall, when he was considered to be the nation’s most endangered Democrat. Instead of playing it safe, he staked his candidacy on affordability issues, particularly subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. In the midst of the longest government shutdown on record, Ossoff held firm: He would not vote to reopen the federal government unless the tax credits were restored.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Other Democratic candidates got the message. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan proved steadfast in linking the billions in federal funding that continue to subsidize Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza to skyrocketing consumer prices on the homefront. Another physician, Dr. Annie Andrews, who defeated Graham, unabashedly campaigned on creating a healthcare public option and gun control measures in South Carolina — and won.

    Right now, Democrats are feeling the wind at their backs. But after the excitement fades from tonight’s successes, they will realize they are now facing an even bigger challenge: To stay true to the mandate they have been given by voters, grudgingly in some cases, and to not, as they have done so often in the past, slip on the proverbial banana peel that is always waiting for them around the corner.

    Throughout his campaign for the Senate, Paxton was fond of saying, “If we lose Texas, we lose America.” Tonight, Democrats put Texas solidly in their column — and America is still standing.

    Latest Update: The American Genius of Madden

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, hang on at the start of David O.
    • The key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football.
    • Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, hang on at the start of David O. Russell’s Madden, as its story of the Oakland Raiders football coach John Madden shifts between semidocumentary and biopic. Russell’s uneven, sketchy narrative steadily turns into a probing human comedy. It’s also a slyly monumental tale of American genius found in an Everyman’s commonplace ambition.

    The key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football. Cage enters the mindset of a sports fanatic who is also an artist, devising plays and strategies that, considering his size and vision, earn him the nickname “Buddha.” But this is not one of those freak-outs that Cage is known for; he seems to transform himself into John Candy — broad-beamed with a tuft of blond hair and a convincing smile. Cage commits to this genial eccentric who, despite his unreachable idiosyncrasy, is harmless, lovable yet tough — an authentic, original American.

    Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend. This thick-and-thin Laurel-and-Hardy pair sustain an unlikely partnership. It’s one of the most remarkable depictions of brotherhood in movies — a friendship that persists over temperamental tensions, even after Madden leaves the team and pursues media entrepreneurship to sustain his love of the sport. Madden the broadcaster converts his playbook ingenuity and follows his father’s advice: “Get away with doing what you love for as long as you possibly can.”.

    Russell redeems himself with the oddest-yet-normal collection of American eccentrics. Acting on the edge of parody, Cage and Bale, with their uncanny sincerity, reward Russell’s interest in quirkiness. (Madden hears Davis’s voice in his head.) The fascinating scoundrels of Russell’s terrific American Hustle were preoccupied with manipulating one another. Here, friendship, comradeship, teamwork, and family complications are genuinely recognizable. Scenes that emulate a documentary approach — Madden’s wife Virginia (gung ho comedienne Kathryn Hahn) rivals Jennifer Lawrence’s volatility when speaking directly to the camera — satirize realism to fulfill the non-cynical view of national character that Russell fumbled in the bohemian sojourn of Amsterdam. No wonder De Niro is left out of this particular silver-lined playbook.

    Nicolas Cage (John Madden) in Madden.

    Chuck Zlotnick/Amazon MGM Studios.

    In a recent development, the patchwork of styles in Madden suggests that Russell investigates American eccentricity as he goes along, finding his way back to the coast-to-coast realness that made his Flirting with Disaster so exhilarating (as in Madden’s surreal, unapologetic pitch for the unique holiday dish the Turducken). Russell adopts Madden’s football-analysis style, such as on-screen telestrator vectors, to humorously examine Madden’s own career shifts and twists of personality (Madden instructing his players, or meeting colleagues Pat Summerall, Howard Cosell, and Bob Costas).

    In a recent development, A dull-witted filmmaker, say James Cameron, would choose an “immersive” style for a movie concerned with the gestalt of football. But Russell’s film is also about the phenomenon of a sport that becomes a vanguard of technology and culture. Madden is pursued by Trip Hawkins (John Mulaney), founder of video game tech giant EA (Electronic Arts), who wants to translate Madden’s football theories for a latest generation of at-home fans and gamers. Hawkins’s proposal is scored to Beethoven’s Ninth — another example of Russell’s wit, matching the film’s eclectic score from Barry White and Talking Heads to N.W.A. (“You don’t want to know what that means,” Davis says to Madden.).

    It has been revealed that through Madden and Hawkins’s acumen, Russell treats the discovery of a latest world as an aftereffect of folk intelligence and ingenuity. Genius is kidded when Hawkins’s team of four-eyed computer nerds demonstrate jock potential after applying Madden’s plays to their algorithms. It’s a sweet way of conveying the phenomenon that would turn EA’s Madden NFL video game franchise into a $4 billion enterprise (some estimates raise that into double digits), with annual compensation going to the Madden family estate.

    More important, Russell (who co-wrote the script with Cambron Clark) sees Madden as a visionary who proudly summarizes TV sportscasting as “They state the obvious, which is f***ing boring.” My only complaint is that Robert Richardson’s photography tends toward frowzy (perhaps deliberately aping TV docs), not as splendid as Oliver Stone’s Any Given Sunday — the greatest football movie ever made.

    It has been revealed that madden itself shares biopic sensibility with John Ford’s The Wings of Eagles, respectfully eschewing its subject’s mortality for an optimistic appreciation of a man’s potential. It is unique to American character and the experience of competition and dreams of the NFL Hall of Fame that Madden shared with Al Davis. Russell’s tribute comes complete with a motto: “You make people feel good and alive and good to be American, and I’m not standing in the way of that.” Thus Russell proves his own resilience and the achievement of a new folkloric genre struggling to emerge.

    Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of Newly introduced Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

    On “The American Genius of Madden”.

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, remarked additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that the Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    According to recent reports, as they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    In a recent development, “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    Recent findings suggest that as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    Recent findings suggest that as with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    According to recent reports, last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they stated they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    Industry observers note that on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    Recent findings suggest that “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., mentioned Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    Recent findings suggest that as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    Recent findings suggest that the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    According to recent reports, john M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    Sen. Susan Collins, the five-term Republican from Maine, called her opponent Troy Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, to concede Tuesday night. The Associated Press called the election just after midnight, with Jackson leading by about six percentage points.

    It has been revealed that despite nearly 30 years in the Senate, Collins has been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents, a smaller pebble in the blue avalanche that wiped out MAGA candidates in the midterm elections. She was the lone Senate Republican to represent a state that former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. She lost despite her efforts to distance herself from President Donald Trump. Her campaign claims she has never voted for the president and reportedly refused his help with her run.

    That hasn’t stopped her from often playing a key role in Trump’s agenda, casting a critical vote in Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court. Kavanaugh would later join the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to an abortion. Indeed, Collins’ position on reproductive rights seems to have played a key role in her defeat. Collins received support from Trump despite her efforts, according to reporting from ProPublica earlier this year, which revealed how an FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating Collins before Trump killed the case.

    According to recent reports, as for Jackson, he first ran for office in 2000 as a Republican for the Maine House of Representatives, but lost. He ran again as an independent two years later and won, becoming the first non-Democrat to represent the area since the late ‘70s.

    Recent findings suggest that before delegates at a state convention chose Jackson in July, Collins was originally running against oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary with support from progressive leaders. But controversies surrounding Platner continued to pile up, and he finally withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault allegations.

    Recent findings suggest that riyadh’s hotels lost their peak season when the airport shut. With BA, Cathay Pacific and others suspended into the new year and Houthi strikes still hitting the capital, the recovery hasn’t started.

    Industry observers note that riyadh hotels had one of their worst months of the year in October. A temporary shutdown of the city’s main airport cut off inbound demand just as peak season started.

    Occupancy fell 34.7 percentage points year over year to 34.3% from 69%, according to CoStar’s STR. Only March had lower occupancy, at 28.3%. Average daily rate dropped 29.9% to $190 and revenue per available room (RevPAR) fell 65.1% to $65.

    “October and November are usually the peak season months for Riyadh, so the impact is much bigger,” stated Kostas Nikolaidis, associate account director for Middle East and Africa at STR.

    The October demand collapse traces back to an attack on King Khalid International Airport. The airport closed after an attack on Oct. 10 that Saudi authorities mentioned killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Some 86% of scheduled Riyadh departures were canceled between Oct. 8 and late October, according to Cirium data, Skift repor.

    Americans should expect their federal agencies to be staffed by experts who gather evidence meticulously before proposing regulations disinterestedly. But that’s not what the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has done when it comes to personalized pricing.

    Last month, the FTC ordered nine major companies — Delta Air Lines, Uber, and Instacart among them — “to provide detailed information that will allow the agency to study the use of personal data to set prices and compensation.” The agency, however, seems to have reached its conclusions already, given the contents of both its order and an enforcement policy proposed in August, which appears partial against personalized pricing and the businesses that employ it.

    #19492. Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1080 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was originally published on The Conversation.
    • Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth unveiled on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone.
    • The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was originally published on The Conversation.

    Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth unveiled on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later stated, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”.

    The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.

    For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

    Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

    It has been revealed that and that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

    For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

    But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

    As Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

    As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

    Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”.

    And then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

    In a recent development, borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

    Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”.

    Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

    Sources indicate that on the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

    Trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

    The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

    It is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

    Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

    Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

    Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

    In a recent development, the deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia shows – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

    Matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison.

    #19490. The petty joy of a blue election night

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1465 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    The petty joy of a blue election night

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow.
    • Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.
    • Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

    Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

    Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”.

    Recent findings suggest that shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

    So we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

    According to recent reports, “If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

    “You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

    Industry observers note that election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

    Recent findings suggest that neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

    So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue showed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

    Sources indicate that “What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”.

    And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

    Peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

    It has been revealed that most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Significant Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood. On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his latest network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    In a recent development, but Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

    It has been revealed that still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”.

    Once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

    According to recent reports, this is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he said.

    So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

    It was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. New Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

    Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

    Sources indicate that once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

    But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she noted, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”.

    So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory said, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”.

    Sources indicate that that moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he said. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”.

    Industry observers note that but by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

Gary Peters, whose departure created one of the most consequential open-seat contests of the midterm elections. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, campaigned on expanding access to health care and lowering costs, while Rogers, a former congressman and House Intelligence Committee chairman, emphasized manufacturing jobs, tax cuts and his alignment with President Donald Trump.

    Industry observers note that the race took an unexpected turn just two days before Election Day when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the party’s August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers during an appearance at a Detroit church.

    In a recent development, the endorsement stunned Michigan Democrats, prompting condemnation from party leaders and resignations among Stevens’ staff. Stevens cited disagreements with El-Sayed over Israel and his campaign’s direction, while Democrats accused her of undermining their nominee in a critical Senate contest.

    El-Sayed sought to move past the controversy, urging supporters to focus on voting. His campaign reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, while Michigan Democratic officials said the endorsement had prompted an increase in volunteers. Rogers, meanwhile, highlighted Stevens’ support in the campaign’s final days.

    More than 2.3 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Monday, according to The Associated Press, raising questions about how much the late-breaking controversy could influence the outcome.

    Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan strategy Thursday to adopt latest rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    According to recent reports, van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a plan from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

    Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

    Recent findings suggest that “I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen said. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”.

    The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

    Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a newly introduced suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move promptly.

    Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

    At the earlier appearance, Daines remarked that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

    “We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines mentioned.

    Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

    But Democrats have been debating whether to use their fresh majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

    Recent findings suggest that democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

    A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines initiative.

    Schumer has stated he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

    Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

    “I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the substantial things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen remarked.
